title: MYP eAssessment Timetable Explained for 2026
summary: MYP eAssessment timetable explained for students and parents, including 2026 dates, exam sessions, subjects, ePortfolios, and planning advice.
body_markdown:
A student looking at the **MYP eAssessment timetable** often sees a wall of dates. A parent may see something different: transport, sleep, revision plans, and several opportunities to ask, “Are you sure that is the right day?”


The useful answer is simple. The International Baccalaureate publishes an official schedule for each MYP examination session, but your school turns that global schedule into the local timetable you actually follow. For May 2026, students and parents should consult the IB’s[official MYP exam schedule page](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/middle-years-programme/assessment-and-exams/onscreen-examinations/exam-schedule/) and then confirm every date, start time, room, and arrival instruction with their MYP coordinator.


This distinction matters. The IB schedule tells you when an examination is assigned internationally. Your school tells you when to arrive and where to sit.


### MYP eAssessment timetable at a glance


Use this checklist before building a revision calendar:


- Download the schedule for the correct session and year, such as May 2026.
- Identify only the subjects for which you are registered.
- Distinguish on-screen examinations from ePortfolio components.
- Check whether each examination is in the morning or afternoon session.
- Obtain the precise local start and arrival times from your school.
- Confirm subject language and level where relevant.
- Ask about approved access arrangements well before the examination period.
- Treat the school’s candidate timetable as your final practical guide.


A student asks for the school timetable while a parent operates an oversized exam mission-control console


*One calendar is useful. Turning the kitchen into mission control is optional.*


### What the timetable actually covers


MYP eAssessment is the optional external assessment available in the final year of the **IB Middle Years Programme** . It is not one identical digital test covering everything a student has studied.


Instead, external assessment can involve two different forms:


Assessment form What students should expect


On-screen examination A scheduled examination completed using a computer under supervised conditions


ePortfolio Coursework or performance evidence produced and submitted according to deadlines managed by the school


According to the IB’s overview of[MYP assessment and examinations](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/middle-years-programme/assessment-and-exams/) , on-screen examinations are used for language and literature, individuals and societies, sciences, mathematics, and interdisciplinary learning. Language acquisition combines an on-screen examination with internally assessed speaking work. Arts, design, and physical and health education use ePortfolios.


That is why students should not expect every subject to appear as a conventional appointment on the examination schedule. An ePortfolio has its own production, authentication, and submission process. Its important dates will usually come through the school rather than appearing like a single morning examination.


### How to read the official MYP schedule


Imagine an MYP student, Sam, opening the schedule and highlighting every row containing the word “mathematics.” That is a reasonable beginning, but it is not enough. Sam must match the timetable entry to the exact registration held by the school.


### Start with the correct examination session


The IB publishes separate schedules for upcoming sessions. Check the month and year at the top of the document before recording anything. A saved file from an earlier cohort may look convincing while being completely irrelevant.


The IB’s exam schedule page currently provides the **May 2026 MYP examination schedule** . Because schedules and administrative guidance can be updated, use the current file linked by the IB rather than relying on a screenshot, forwarded message, or unofficial calendar.


### Find the subject and language


Read the complete row, not merely the first familiar word. Depending on the available entries and your registration, the row may identify a subject, language, or other variation that determines whether it belongs to you.


Parents can help here without taking over. Ask the student to compare the schedule with the candidate registration details supplied by the coordinator. Any mismatch should be raised with the school immediately.


### Read morning and afternoon as session labels


“Morning” and “afternoon” do not give every student worldwide one universal clock time. Schools operate within IB requirements while communicating the exact local arrangements to candidates.


Never calculate a start time from another country’s timetable or assume that a friend at a different school will begin at precisely the same moment. Your coordinator’s instructions determine your arrival time. Arriving at the listed start time may already be too late if the school requires candidates to check in earlier.


### Separate duration from arrival time


The duration of an examination tells you how long the assessed session lasts. It does not include travel, registration, equipment checks, seating, or instructions.


A useful personal calendar therefore needs at least four fields:


Field Example of what to record


Assessment Exact registered subject


Date and session Official date plus morning or afternoon


School arrival time Time communicated by the coordinator


Preparation note Equipment, room, or access arrangement


### Why your school timetable is the decisive document


International schedules create consistency. Local timetables make that consistency workable.


Your school knows the local time, examination room, device arrangements, supervision plan, and candidate list. It also manages approved inclusive access arrangements and communicates what students may bring into the room. Those details cannot be inferred safely from a general online summary.


The best approach is to keep two documents together:


1. The current official IB schedule, which lets you verify the examination date and session.
2. The individual candidate timetable from school, which gives you actionable local instructions.


If they appear to conflict, do not choose one yourself. Send both to the MYP coordinator and ask for written clarification.


### Turning dates into a calm revision plan


A timetable is not a study plan. It becomes one only when a student works backward from it.


Suppose Sam has science followed shortly by mathematics. Spending the entire week before science on that subject may feel disciplined, but it pushes mathematics into a narrow and stressful gap. A better plan keeps both subjects active, then gradually increases the emphasis on the earlier assessment.


### Build the plan in three layers


**First, map fixed commitments.** Add every examination, school deadline, ePortfolio milestone, journey, and non-negotiable commitment.


**Second, diagnose the work.** Use targeted questions and grading feedback to identify weaknesses. RevisionDojo’s Questionbank and AI grading tools can turn “revise science” into a more useful instruction, such as reviewing data interpretation or practising the construction of a supported conclusion.


**Third, rehearse the experience.** Timed Mock Exams and Predicted Papers help students practise sustained decision-making rather than isolated recall. Study Notes and Flashcards support shorter review sessions, while AI Chat can help untangle a concept that remains unclear. These resources are most useful when they answer a diagnosed need, not when they merely fill time.


RevisionDojo also brings together a Coursework Library and Tutors, which can be valuable when ePortfolio planning or teacher feedback reveals a specific gap. The goal is not to use every feature every day. It is to choose the smallest tool that solves the current problem.


### Common timetable mistakes to avoid


The most expensive timetable mistakes usually begin as small assumptions.


**Using an unofficial copy.** A social post may omit a page or preserve an outdated version. Begin with the IB website.


**Confusing IB Diploma dates with MYP dates.** Both may be described informally as “IB exams,” but they are different programmes with different schedules. One relevant RevisionDojo guide covers the[IB May 2026 exam schedule](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-may-2026-exam-schedule-full-timetable-dates-and-planning-guide) , but MYP candidates must use the separate MYP schedule linked by the IB.


**Expecting every MYP subject to appear as an on-screen examination.** Some externally assessed components use ePortfolios instead.


**Ignoring local instructions.** The date alone does not tell you when to arrive, which room to use, or what equipment is permitted.


**Planning revision by subject size alone.** The order and spacing of assessments should influence how revision time is distributed.


### The timetable is a boundary, not a prediction


An assessment calendar cannot tell a student how the month will feel. It only marks the boundaries within which choices will be made.


For students, the next step is to highlight their registered assessments and build a backward plan. For parents, it is to verify logistics, protect sleep, and let the student retain ownership of the work. Both should ask the school when anything remains uncertain.


RevisionDojo is designed for the part that follows: converting those dates into focused practice through Questionbank tasks, Study Notes, Flashcards, AI Chat, grading tools, Predicted Papers, Mock Exams, the Coursework Library, and expert Tutors. A timetable tells you when you will be assessed. Good preparation decides what you do before then.
